Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade K, Step 1 Introduce.

Yesterday, we learned that the first step in writing a report is researching—collecting facts from texts. Today, I'm going to teach you more about how to JOT THOSE FACTS AS SHORT, CLEAR FACT PHRASES during the research step.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grades K-2, Step 2A Tell. This content is near-identical across grades K, 1, and 2.

Yesterday, we discussed that we cannot remember everything we research about a topic, so we must record the information we learn from texts. Review the 4-step process for collecting research:
1. Read the text carefully.
2. Find a fact.
3. Say the fact out loud.
4. Jot down the fact phrase.

Yesterday, we practiced reading 1-2 sentences (Step 1), finding the fact hidden inside it (Step 2), and restating that fact orally in 1-4 words (Step 3), before jotting it down in writing (Step 4).

WHAT the skill is: "Jotting" means writing something down quickly and simply. That is different from writing sentences. We WRITE sentences, but we JOT research facts. Research notes are just for you—the writer. Your audience will never see them. They will only read your finished report. Just like a grocery list is only for the shopper, research notes only need to make sense to you. So when we take notes from texts, we don't spend time making them neat, pretty, or perfect—even the spelling doesn't have to be perfect.

Contrast sentences vs. research facts:
Sentences: Are complete thoughts. Use capitals & end marks. Use our best handwriting.
Research facts: Are 1-4 words. Don't use capitals or end marks. Don't use perfect handwriting.

WHY the skill is important: Research notes are reminders of the important facts and details we will later turn into sentences in our report. Since we often research over several days, there is time between when we jot the fact and when we use it. So we must give ourselves enough information to understand it later. But here's the tricky part: we can't write too much, and we can't write too little. We need enough words to remember what the fact means. And while we don't need perfect handwriting, we still need to be able to read what we wrote. (Could make a connection to Goldilocks—just right.)

Let's think about a grocery list again. When I make a grocery list, I can't just write "cheese." That's too vague. Do I need slices for sandwiches? Shredded for tacos? Cheese cubes for a snack? I have to jot just enough to remember what I meant. And if I write it so messy I can't read it, it won't help me at all. Research notes work the same way—just enough words, written clearly enough to read later.

HOW the skill works: Young writers often use paper with small boxes, small slips of paper, or sticky notes to jot their fact phrases. This smaller paper reminds us NOT to write whole sentences during the research stage. Introduce ways to jot fact phrases in 1-4 words:
- Omit a, an, the.
- If a person is referenced often, use only his initials.
- Use the ampersand (&) for "and."
- Use an equal sign (=) to show 2 things are the same.
- Use a long dash to add a detail or description.

The quicker we can jot fact phrases during research, the more information we gather for our report—and the more our reader learns about the topic.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grades 3-5, Step 2A Tell. This content is near-identical across grades 3, 4, and 5.

Yesterday, we discussed that we cannot remember everything we research about a topic, so we must record the information we learn from texts. (Review the 4-step process for collecting research.)
1. Read the text carefully.
2. Find a fact.
3. Say the fact out loud.
4. Jot down the fact phrase.

Yesterday, we practiced reading 1-2 sentences (Step 1), finding the fact hidden inside it (Step 2), and restating that fact orally in 1-4 words (Step 3), before jotting it down in writing (Step 4).

WHAT the skill is: "Jotting" means writing something down quickly and simply. That is different from writing sentences. We WRITE sentences, but we JOT research facts. Research notes are just for you—the writer. Your audience will never see them. Just like a grocery list is only for the shopper, research notes only need to make sense to you.

Contrast sentences vs. research facts:
Sentences: Are complete thoughts. Use capitals & end marks. Use our best handwriting.
Research facts: Are 1-4 words. Don't use capitals or end marks. Don't use perfect handwriting.

WHY the skill is important: Research notes are reminders of the important facts and details we will later turn into sentences. Because we often research over several days, there is time between when we jot a fact and when we use it. So we must give ourselves enough information to understand it later—but not so much that we slow down our research. That means we can't write too much, and we can't write too little. We don't need perfect handwriting, but we do need to be able to read what we wrote. The goal is to jot efficiently.

"Efficient" means fast and helpful. If we use too many words, it's not efficient. If we write too little and it doesn't make sense later, it's not helpful. If it's too messy to read, it won't work. Efficient jotting is the right balance—just enough words, written clearly enough to read later.

HOW the skill works: Provide ways for students to communicate bulleted facts in 4 or less words:
- Omit a, an, the from every fact phrase.
- If a person is referenced often, use only his initials.
- Use the ampersand (&) for "and."
- Use abbreviations or text-message shortcuts (w = with, bc = because).
- Use an arrow between 2 things to show how one became, turned into, evolved, produced, etc. the other.
- Use an equal sign (=) to show 2 things are the same.
- Use a long dash to add a detail or description to something.

The quicker we jot fact phrases during research, the more information we gather for our report—and the more our reader learns about the topic.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade K, Step 2B Show. Topic: Space. Teacher think-aloud demonstrating how to jot fact phrases using the 4-step process.

"Let me show you how to jot a fact phrase using the 4-step process from yesterday."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text on a topic students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (This could be the same passage from yesterday, just reference a different excerpt during the model. See Source 1, p1 on Space.)

Step 1: Read a text. "Space is the place above our planet."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the fact in that sentence? What did that say? "Space is above our planet."
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. What are the most important words? The word "space" and where it is: "above our planet." That's 4 words. That tells where space is. Yes, that works. And since I'm not writing a sentence, I could use an equals sign instead of "is."
Step 4: Jot it down. Talk to yourself while writing only "space = above our planet" on the note-taking paper.

That's one fact phrase. Now I do it again with another sentence—read, find, say, jot.

Step 1: Read. "Earth is the planet where we live."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the fact? (Point.) "Earth is the planet where we live." That's the fact. Let me try... "Earth is the planet where we live." That's a lot more than 4 words! I know I don't need to write the whole sentence, but I also don't need to write facts I already know. I already wrote Earth is a planet. What is the new fact here? (Point to "where we live.")
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. Say that again counting the words on your fingers: "live on Earth." That's only 3 words.
Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) Live... on... Earth. Short. Readable. That is a good fact phrase.

Today, we are learning how to quickly jot down fact phrases. The more fact phrases we collect during research, the stronger our informative report will be later.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 1, Step 2B Show. Topic: US Symbols. Teacher think-aloud demonstrating how to jot fact phrases using the 4-step process.

"Let me show you how to jot a fact phrase using the 4-step process from yesterday."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text on a topic students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (This could be the same passage from yesterday, just reference a different excerpt during the model. See Source 1, p1 on US Symbols.)

Step 1: Read. "It has 13 stripes that are red and white."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the true fact? (Point.) "13 stripes." That's a fact.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. Let me try... "It has 13 red and white stripes." Too many words. I don't need "it has" because I'm not writing a sentence. What are the most important words? "13 stripes" and "red and white." That's what I need to jot. Oooh, I could use the shortcut for "and," too. Yes. "13 red & white stripes." That works.
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself while writing only "13 red & white stripes" on the note-taking paper.

That's one fact phrase. Now I do it again with another sentence—read, find, say, jot.

Step 1: Read. "The 13 stripes stand for the first 13 states."
Step 2: Find a fact. "13 stripes stand for first 13 states." Whoa. That's too long. I already jotted down that the flag has 13 stripes. I don't need to write that again. What is the new fact here? (Point.) The number of stripes matches the first 13 states. That's important.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. "First 13 states." That's only three words. That tells me what they stand for. And that's only 3 words. Good.
Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) First... 13... states. Short. Readable. That is a good fact phrase.

Today, we are learning how to quickly jot down fact phrases. The more fact phrases we collect during research, the stronger our informative report will be later.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 2, Step 2B Show. Topic: Public Services. Teacher think-aloud demonstrating how to jot fact phrases using the 4-step process.

"Let me show you how to jot a fact phrase using the 4-step process from yesterday."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text on a topic students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (This could be the same passage from yesterday, just reference a different excerpt during the model. See Source 1, p1 on Public Services.)

Step 1: Read. "Recreation is a public service that cities and towns provide."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the important fact in this sentence? (Point.) "Recreation is a public service." That's the main fact. The rest explains who provides it.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. But I know I shouldn't write all of that... (Use fingers to count each word as you say it.) "Recreation is a public service." WHOA! That's too long. I don't need "is" or "a" because I'm not writing a sentence. I just need the important words? "Recreation" and "public service." That's 3 words. Clear and strong. That works.
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself while writing only "recreation public service" on the note-taking paper.

That's one fact phrase. Now I do it again with another sentence—read, find, say, jot.

Step 1: Read. "They build places where families can play and exercise."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the true fact? (Point.) "Build places for families." That's the heart of the sentence.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. Let me try... "Cities build places where families can play and exercise." Too many words. What are the key words? "play & exercise" and maybe "family." That's 4 words. And I can use the "and" shortcut to jot even faster!
Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) Families... play... &... exercise. Short. Neat. That is a good fact phrase.

Today, we are learning how to quickly jot down fact phrases. The more fact phrases we collect during research, the stronger our informative report will be later.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 3, Step 2B Show. Topic: Simple Machines. Teacher think-aloud demonstrating how to jot fact phrases using the 4-step process.

"Let me show you how to jot a fact phrase using the 4-step process from yesterday."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text on a topic students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (This could be the same passage from yesterday, just reference a different excerpt during the model. See Source 1, p1 on Simple Machines.)

Step 1: Read. "A pulley is a wheel with a groove and a rope."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the important fact in this sentence? (Point.) "Pulley is a wheel with a groove and a rope." That tells what a pulley is. That's what's important.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. Now I don't want to write that whole sentence—it's too long. I need to find the most important words. (Point.) "Wheel with groove and rope"—that's what a pulley is. Oooh, instead of writing "is," I can use an equal sign. And instead of writing "with" and "and," I can use the shortcuts.
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself while writing only "pulley = wheel w/ groove & rope" on the note-taking paper. Point out that there are still only 4 whole words written.

That's one fact phrase. Now I do it again with another sentence—read, find, say, jot.

Step 1: Read. "Construction workers use long slanted boards to move heavy materials to higher places."
Step 2: Find a fact. What is the fact? (Point.) "Use long slanted boards to move heavy materials." That's what construction workers do.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. I know I don't need the whole sentence. So what are the most important words? "Construction workers... slanted boards... move heavy materials." But that's still too many words. How can I make it more efficient? I don't need to write "workers use" or "to move." I can show that action with an arrow. I also don't need "materials to higher places"—just "heavy." Let me shrink it more. "Slanted boards (arrow) heavy construction." Oooh, I can shorten "construction" to "constr."
So I'll say it like this: "Slanted boards (arrow) heavy, constr." That keeps the idea & is fast.
Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) Slanted... boards... (draw arrow)... heavy... (comma)... constr.

Today, we are learning how to quickly jot down fact phrases. The more fact phrases we collect during research, the stronger our informative report will be later.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 4, Step 2B Show. Topic: Ben Franklin. Teacher think-aloud demonstrating how to jot fact phrases using the 4-step process.

"Let me show you how to jot a fact phrase using the 4-step process from yesterday."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text on a topic students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (This could be the same passage from yesterday, just reference a different excerpt during the model. See Source 1, p1 on Ben Franklin.)

Step 1: Read. "In one famous experiment, he flew a kite during a thunderstorm and attached a key to the string to show that lightning is a form of electricity."
Step 2: Find a fact. What's important here? (Point.) "Famous experiment, flew a kite, attached a key, lightning is electricity."
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. Let me try to shrink each of those down into 1-2 words. I don't need "famous" or "flew." "Kite" and "key" are what's important about the "experiment"... and that it made "electricity." But I can't just write down those 4 separate words; it won't make sense later. I know I can use a plus sign (+) to combine 2 things—like "key" and "kite." And I can use the equal sign (=) to show what happened.
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself while writing only "kite + key = electricity experiment." Point out that there are still only 4 words. Using symbols within the fact phrases helps keep them short and clear.

That's one fact phrase. Now I do it again with another sentence—read, find, say, jot.

Step 1: Read. "Benjamin Franklin was an important leader in early American history. He was born in 1706 in Boston and grew up to become a writer, inventor, scientist, and statesman."
Step 2: Find a fact. The first sentence tells me he was an important leader—but that's broad. I'll likely have other notes about his leadership. The second sentence gives me a precise detail: "born in 1706 in Boston." That's concrete and easy to record.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. The key words are the date and place. So I'll shrink it to: "born 1706, Boston."
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself while writing only "born... 1706... (comma)... Boston."

Today, we are learning how to quickly jot down fact phrases. The more fact phrases we collect during research, the stronger our informative report will be later.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 5, Step 2B Show. Topic: Paul Revere. Teacher think-aloud demonstrating how to jot fact phrases using the 4-step process.

"Let me show you how to jot a fact phrase using the 4-step process from yesterday."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text on a topic students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (This could be the same passage from yesterday, just reference a different excerpt during the model. See Source 1, p1 on Paul Revere.)

Step 1: Read. "Paul Revere was an important leader during the American Revolution. A revolution is a time when people fight to change their government."
Step 2: Find a fact. What literal facts do I want to record? From the first sentence: "important leader" and "American Revolution." The second sentence defines revolution, but my note card is about Paul Revere's role. Both connect to him and the Revolution.
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. The whole sentence is too long. What are the strongest words? "Paul Revere," "leader," "American Revolution." I don't need the full definition—just the key term. I can shorten "American Revolution" to "Am. Rev." to save space. So my fact phrase will be: "Paul Revere = leader, Am. Revolution." That's four clear parts. It keeps the important words and stays efficient.
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself while writing the bulleted phrase: "Paul... Revere... (equals)... leader... (comma)... Am.... Rev."

That's one fact phrase. Now I do it again with another sentence—read, find, say, jot.

Step 1: Read. "Paul Revere is most famous for his midnight ride in April 1775. When he learned that British troops were marching toward Lexington and Concord, he rode through the night to warn colonial leaders that the British were coming."
Step 2: Find a fact. His "midnight ride" "warned colonial leaders."
Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. I can shrink "colonial leaders" to "colonists." And I could use the long dash to connect "midnight ride—warned colonists." Hmm... I'm also thinking that dates are important in history. I could put "Apr 1775" at the top of the note.
Step 4: Jot. Talk to yourself as you write "Apr 1775" at the top of the note. Then "midnight ride—warned colonists" below it.

Today, we are learning how to quickly jot down fact phrases. The more fact phrases we collect during research, the stronger our informative report will be later.

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade K, Step 3 Interact. Topic: Weather.

"Help me with another example."

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 1, p3 on Weather. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "Precipitation is water that falls from the sky. It can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail."
Fact phrase: precipitation = rain, snow

Original: "A blizzard is a big snowstorm with strong wind and blowing snow."
Fact phrase: blizzard = big snowstorm

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 1, Step 3 Interact. Topic: Space.

"Help me with another example."

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 1, p3 on Space. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "The Sun gives us sunlight. Sunlight makes our days bright and warm."
Fact phrase: sunlight = bright, warm

Original: "In summer, we have longer days with more sunlight. In winter, we have shorter days with less sunlight."
Fact phrase: summer longer; winter shorter

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 2, Step 3 Interact. Topic: Habitats.

"Help me with another example."

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 1, p3 on Habitats. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "The forest floor is dark and damp. Decomposition happens there."
Fact phrase: forest floor = dark & damp

Original: "In deserts, cacti store water in their thick stems."
Fact phrase: cacti stems store water

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 3, Step 3 Interact. Topic: Fossils.

"Help me with another example."

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 1, p3 on Fossils. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "Fossils can form over millions of years. Layers of mud and sand cover the remains."
Fact phrase: layers mud/sand (arrow) fossils

Original: "Paleontologists use picks, brushes, and mirrors."
Fact phrase: paleontologists/scientists—picks, brushes

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 4, Step 3 Interact. Topic: European Exploration.

"Help me with another example."

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 1, p3 on European Exploration. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "Some explorers wanted to spread their religion. Missionaries hoped to teach others about their beliefs."
Fact phrase: explorers/missionaries—spread religion

Original: "Explorers were searching for wealth, such as gold, silver, spices, and other precious metals."
Fact phrase: wealth (arrow) gold, silver, spices, metals

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grade 5, Step 3 Interact. Topic: Earth's Spheres.

"Help me with another example."

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 1, p3 on Earth's Spheres. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "The geosphere includes all the solid parts of Earth. This includes rocks, minerals, and landforms."
Fact phrase: geosphere = rocks, minerals

Original: "The geosphere is made of layers called the crust, mantle, and core. The crust is the thin outer layer where we live."
Fact phrase: geosphere—crust, mantle, core

Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 2 of 3) — Grades K-5, Step 4 Close. This closing script is identical across all six grade levels (K-5).

"Writers, today we learned ways to quickly jot down fact phrases from our research. During Independent Writing Time, your job is to jot down as many fact phrases as you can. Let's push ourselves to see how many we can collect. We want many details. Let's go be writers!"

(Provide a previously-read text on a third topic—but not one students will write a report on. Students may work in pairs to identify facts, but each student must jot down his own fact phrases.)
